theme: I cry aloud to God; I remember your deeds
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 77. You read this psalm in Unit 6. This time read it as the prayer of someone who has lived through national catastrophe. Notice how the psalmist moves from his own distress to the memory of the exodus.
settingTheScene: Psalm 77 is a psalm of Asaph, and it belongs with the other Asaph psalms of this unit. You read it earlier as an example of the discipline of remembering. Now, at the end of the divided kingdom and the fall of Israel, it takes on a new weight. When God’s people were cast into exile, this was the question: has his steadfast love ceased? And the answer given is: remember the exodus.
observation: “I cry aloud to God, aloud to God, and he will hear me” (v. 1).
“In the day of my trouble I seek the Lord; in the night my hand is stretched out without wearying; my soul refuses to be comforted” (v. 2).
“I remember God, and I am troubled; I meditate, and my spirit faints” (v. 3).
“Will the Lord spurn forever, and never again be favorable? Has his steadfast love forever ceased?” (vv. 7-8).
“Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has he in anger shut up his compassion?” (v. 9).
“Then I said, This is my grief: that the right hand of the Most High has changed” (v. 10).
“I will remember the deeds of the LORD; yes, I will remember your wonders of old” (v. 11).
“Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters; yet your footprints were unseen. You led your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron” (vv. 19-20).
interpretation:
The psalm is a record of a spiritual struggle. The psalmist cries out. He cannot sleep. His soul “refuses to be comforted.” Even remembering God makes him troubled. This is a striking detail: the thought of God, which should comfort, brings distress because God seems absent. He asks a series of questions that every believer in exile has asked: Will the Lord reject forever? Has his steadfast love ceased? Has he forgotten to be gracious?

These are honest questions, and the Bible includes them. Faith does not require us to suppress doubt. It requires us to bring it to God.

The turn comes in verse 10 and 11. The psalmist says, “This is my grief.” Some read the line as: “It is my weakness that the right hand of the Most High has changed.” The meaning is that he has been looking at the problem from the wrong angle. He decides to change his focus. “I will remember the deeds of the LORD; I will remember your wonders of old.” He deliberately turns his mind from his present trouble to God’s past acts.

He then recounts the exodus. God’s way was in the sea, in the great waters, “yet your footprints were unseen.” This is a striking line. God’s footprints were not visible, but he was there. The people crossed the sea, led by an invisible God. In our own times of darkness, we may not see the footprints, but he is leading.

The psalm ends with a quiet image: “You led your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron.” It is a modest closing line. God leads through ordinary human leaders. The God of the thunder and lightning also leads like a shepherd.

For a people in exile, this was the answer. Remember the exodus. God has rescued before, and he will again.
connection: The exodus is the pattern of the greater salvation in Christ, who leads us out of slavery to sin (Luke 9:31 speaks of his “exodus” in Jerusalem). Hebrews 13:20 calls him the “great shepherd of the sheep.” Jesus walked on the sea, and his footsteps were seen by the disciples in the storm (Mark 6:48-51). 1 Corinthians 10:1-4 describes the passage through the sea as a baptism into Moses.
application:
When you feel that God has changed, practice remembering. Write a list of his past deeds in your life.

Bring your honest questions to God. Do not edit them.

Look back for “footprints” you did not see at the time.
prayerPrompts: Cry aloud to God and tell him what your soul refuses to be comforted about.
Remember one of his wonders and rest on it.
Thank him that he leads like a flock, even through unseen footprints.
